title: Nine Justices, Nine Styles
hook: One scholar coded 5,095 questions from a full Supreme Court term and found each justice interrogates lawyers in a signature way — a fingerprint of how they think about the law.
key_points: Greil coded 5,095 questions from 58 oral arguments in the 2025 term to map each justice's signature style.
Thomas dwells on legal history (about 28% of his questions, near double the average) — the originalist hunt for original meaning.
Alito leans on extreme hypotheticals (~30%); Roberts probes for the 'limiting principle' — where a proposed rule stops.
Kavanaugh weighs real-world consequences; Gorsuch fishes for concessions that pin down a lawyer's position.
Jackson runs Socratic question-chains; Kagan pushes back hardest; Sotomayor asks the most and demands record citations.
Greil's point: the patterns help advocates prepare — and show the public how each justice reasons.
content_html: Every Supreme Court advocate knows the justices ask questions in different ways — but John Greil put numbers to it. Writing for SCOTUSblog, he coded more than 5,000 questions from a full term of oral arguments and found that each justice interrogates lawyers in a signature style that mirrors how they think about the law.
extra_html: Greil analyzed 5,095 questions across 58 oral arguments of the Court's 2025 term, scoring what each question was doing — and the patterns line up with each justice's known approach. Justice Thomas spends about 28% of his questions on historical and legal background, nearly double the Court's average — the mark of his originalist search for a text's original meaning. Justice Alito reaches for extreme hypotheticals (around 30% of his questions) to stress-test where a proposed rule would lead, while Chief Justice Roberts hunts for the "limiting principle": the point at which a rule stops, so the Court can judge its long-term reach. Justice Kavanaugh weighs practical, real-world consequences; Justice Gorsuch fishes for concessions that pin down a party's position. Justice Sotomayor, a former trial judge, asks the most questions of anyone (901 in the term) and demands citations to the case record at more than twice the average rate; Justice Kagan pushes back on unsatisfying answers more than any colleague. Justice Jackson favors Socratic sequences — chains of questions that walk an advocate toward a conclusion — and Justice Barrett is the likeliest to pick up and finish a thread a colleague started. Greil's argument is practical as well as descriptive: knowing these fingerprints helps lawyers prepare for specific justices, and it lets the public see how the Court actually reasons its way to a decision. (This card describes U.S. Supreme Court practice specifically.)

related.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
related.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

related.title: Not All Dissents Are Created Equal
related.hook: Dissent tallies treat a one-line 'I would deny' the same as a fully reasoned opinion. One scholar sorted 386 of them on the emergency docket — and found about half were just bare votes.

related.title: Why No Cameras in the Supreme Court?
related.hook: You can read every Supreme Court ruling, but you can't watch the arguments on video. The long fight over courtroom cameras is really a fight over judicial transparency.
